extracted.intended_audience: Senators, congressional staff, patent practitioners, damages experts, and judges considering patent damages and post-grant review reform
extracted.subtask_description: A set of proposed statutory and evidentiary standards for calculating patent damages, regulating expert testimony, sequencing trial issues, and structuring post-grant review proceedings in U.S. patent litigation. Focuses on discouraging crude valuation methods and improving gatekeeping of expert evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty defined as hypothetical negotiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Codifies current Federal Circuit precedent defining a reasonable royalty as the amount that the infringer and patent owner would have agreed to in a hypothetical negotiation at the time infringement began (tracks Rite-Hite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mental framework is inherent in the concept of a 'reasonable royalty' and requires the trier of fact to determine what the parties would have agreed to; the source of bad results is the particular evidence and methods used, not the hypothetical negotiation framework itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: All appropriate Georgia-Pacific factors may be used
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (c) preserves the use of the remaining Georgia-Pacific factors and any other appropriate factor to calculate a reasonable royalty, despite specific codifications and modifications elsewhere in the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill codifies some Georgia-Pacific factors while explicitly allowing other factors to be considered as appropriate in a given case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disfavor standardized measures (rule of thumb/industry averages/IBM 1%-up-to-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (d) bars the use of industry averages, rule-of-thumb profit splits, and other standardized measures to value a patent except under particular circumstances; standardized measures are defined as methods that do not gauge the particular benefits and advantages of the use of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These 'cookie-cutter' methods can produce wildly inaccurate results and are to be disfavored; examples include the 40% rule of thumb, industry average starting points, and the IBM 1%-up-to-5 formula. The subsection restricts Georgia-Pacific factor 12 (rule of thumb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow standardized measure only if invention is primary reason for purchase
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (1) of subsection (d) permits use of a standardized measure (e.g., profit split) only if the patented invention is the primary reason why consumers buy the infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'primary reason' standard is deliberately high (not 'substantial basis') so that only one patent per product would typically meet it; rationale is to avoid awarding bulk profits multiple times to multiple patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established royalties excepted from bar on standardized measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (2) of subsection (d) expressly exempts established royalties from the prohibition on standardized measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Established royalties are widely considered the gold standard for valuing a patent; the explicit exception avoids needless litigation over whether an established royalty is 'based on the benefits and advantages' of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry averages only for confirmation, not as independent method
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (3) of subsection (d) allows industry averages to be used to confirm results produced by other, independently allowable methods, but not as an independent standalone method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'industry average' should not be the primary basis for valuation because licensing data typically reflect only the subset of substantial patents that get licensed, thus tending to overstate minor patents' value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety valve for standardized measures when no other method available
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (4) of subsection (d) permits a standardized measure if no other method is reasonably available to calculate a reasonable royalty and the standardized method is otherwise shown to be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to be rarely used; if one party presents appropriate evidence using a non-standard method, the safety valve cannot be invoked. The clause acknowledges unforeseeable situations where precise economic analysis may be infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-standardized, acceptable valuation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain methodologies are identified as clearly not standardized measures: established royalties, costs of designing around a patent, comparisons to noninfringing alternatives, and cost savings produced by use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods gauge the particular benefits and advantages of the invention and are therefore outside subsection (d)'s restrictions; they are treated as appropriate valuation approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparables restricted and regulated
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (e) restricts use of licenses paid for supposedly comparable patents: comparables may be probative but are often abused and thus are authorized only in conjunction with or to confirm other methods and must be drawn from the same or an analogous technological field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparability is subjective; just because another patent is licensed in the same industry is not alone sufficient. The term 'analogous technological field' is chosen over 'industry' to avoid overbroad definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guideposts for determining economic comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (2) of subsection (e) suggests requiring a showing that the supposed comparable is of similar significance to its licensed product as the patent in suit is to the infringing product, and that the licensed and infringing products have a similar profit margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are guideposts, not exhaustive or mandatory factors; thorough comparability analysis may depend on many other case-specific factors and courts may consider additional or different indicia as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar on using defendant's wealth/profitability to justify damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (f) bars parties from arguing that damages should be based on the wealth or profitability of the defendant as of the time of trial (i.e., 'deep pockets' arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This does not preclude consideration of the infringer's finances at the time of infringement if there is evidence that such information is considered in licensing in the relevant industry; the subsection targets use of trial-time wealth to inflate awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptive sequencing right: decide validity before damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (g) gives either party a presumptive right to demand that validity and infringement be decided before the jury hears arguments about damages, allowing sequencing (not full bifurcation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents plaintiffs from prematurely injecting damages arguments to influence the jury's view of validity and avoids forcing defendants to argue both liability and damages in the same breath; sequencing does not require a second jury but permits completion of pretrial damages activity beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert disclosure: written testimony and underlying data
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (h) requires an expert to provide to the opposing party his written testimony and the data and other information on which his conclusions and methods are based, and also to provide the written testimony to the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplements current procedural rules to prevent experts from testifying about 'custom' without disclosing objective foundations; providing written testimony to the judge facilitates consideration of motions on relevance and admissibility (Daubert motions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded patent-specific Daubert/Rule 702 (Section 299A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 299A creates a patent-specific and expanded Daubert rule by making Rule 702 specific to the Federal Circuit and patent law, requiring development of consistent Rule 702 jurisprudence tailored to patent-damages issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedding Rule 702 in the patent code aims to ensure district courts and the Federal Circuit develop consistent, thorough standards about what damages-calculation methodologies are reliable in patent cases, rather than borrowing non-patent regional circuits' precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional reliability indicia: independent use outside litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 299A adds an indicium of reliability asking whether a theory or technique has been employed independently of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This filters out methodologies that exist only in litigation expert testimony and were never used in actual licensing negotiations; it promotes use of methods that would have been used in a real hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional reliability indicia: consideration of readily available alternative theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 299A adds an indicium requiring that the expert has accounted for readily available alternative theories (e.g., market price of noninfringing alternatives, costs of design-arounds, cost savings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert who ignores precise and objective alternative metrics in favor of subjective, manipulable methods is a sign of bias; this factor helps ensure gatekeeping of biased experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to explain Daubert determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed section 299A(c) requires district courts and circuit courts to explain their Daubert (Rule 702) determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandating explanation should facilitate appellate review of admissibility decisions and development of consistent jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment and JMOL on damages; jury instruction limited to substantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection (i) codifies and reinforces the availability of summary judgment or JMOL on damages issues and requires a court to instruct the jury only on those issues supported by substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids the practice of reading the entire laundry list of Georgia-Pacific factors to the jury; identifying which factors have substantial evidentiary support provides better guidance to the jury and clarifies the record for appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for economic analysis over rough/subjective methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill codifies that all relevant factors may be considered but adopts guidelines and rules that favor the use of an economic analysis of the value of an invention over rough or subjective methodologies such as the rule of thumb, industry averages, or comparables when misused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legislative design aims to promote methods that measure particular benefits and advantages of the patented invention and to reduce systemic occurrences of inflated awards driven by unsound, easy-to-present techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review: two-window structure and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5 authorizes post-grant review proceedings with a first-period proceeding (first-window) in which any invalidity argument can be presented and a second-period proceeding (second-window) limited to novelty and nonobviousness arguments based on patents or printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first-window must be brought within 9 months after issuance; the second window is open for the life of the patent after the 9-month window lapses or after any first-period proceeding concludes. Procedural restrictions are imposed to limit time and expense and to protect patent owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppositional post-grant model with petitioner burden and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill uses an oppositional model for post-grant review (preferred by the PTO) where the burden is on the petitioner to show a claim is not patentable, not on the PTO; this model supports quicker adjudication and predictable deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed section 329(b)(1) mandates completion of post-grant proceedings within one year of institution, with a possible 6-month extension for good cause or second-window joinder; this is intended to avoid interminable delays seen in inter partes reexamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of inter partes reexam and director-initiated reexam
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5(a) repeals procedures for inter partes reexam effective one year after enactment and also repeals director-initiated reexam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for reexam filed before the effective date may continue; director-initiated reexam is repealed to avoid future political pressure being brought on the PTO to attack patents.
